title: Song of Solomon 6:1–3
context: In the WEB headings, the Friends ask where the beloved has gone (6:1), and the Beloved answers that he has gone down to his garden and affirms, “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine” (6:2–3), echoing 2:16.

verses.text: Where has your beloved gone, you fairest among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?
verses.arminianNotes: The WEB heading marks the Friends: “Where has your beloved gone, you fairest among women?” Arminian readers see others wanting to join the search after hearing the beloved’s praise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the praise of chapter 5 drawing others in. Allegorical readers sometimes apply this to the church’s witness attracting others to seek Christ, while literal readers see friends offering help.

verses.text: My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture his flock in the gardens, and to gather lilies.
verses.arminianNotes: Under the heading Beloved: “My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices.” Arminian readers see her knowing where he is, suggesting restored closeness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the search resolved. The garden imagery returns from chapter 4, and readers in this tradition see it as the place of shared love, however the Song is interpreted.

verses.text: I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine. He browses among the lilies.
verses.arminianNotes: “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine.” Arminian readers see mutual belonging freely affirmed, echoing 2:16 with the order reversed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant belonging expressed. Allegorical readers apply it to the bond between Christ and his people, while literal readers see marital faithfulness; readers in both traditions commonly cherish the line.
